bib.title: Chapter 5. Policy Gradient Methods (Reinforcement Learning: Industrial Applications of Intelligent Agents)

question: How can an agent learn a policy directly, via the policy gradient, and how do REINFORCE, baseline, actor-critic and eligibility-trace variants differ?
contributions: Derives the policy gradient theorem (Eq 5-3) and update rule (Eq 5-4)
Logistic and softmax policies and their gradients
REINFORCE, REINFORCE with baseline, n-step actor-critic (A2C), eligibility-trace actor-critic, compared on CartPole
Industrial example: Instacart shopping-cart environment with transfer learning

results.claim: REINFORCE with baseline gave slightly more stable CartPole learning than plain REINFORCE, needing 50 runs for significance.
results.setup: CartPole, linear policy (4 weights), Winder's own runs; gamma and learning rates not in the extracted text (equations lost); baseline is a rolling average of rewards
results.quote: I had to run the experiment over 50 different runs to obtain results that were statistically significant with the same settings.

results.claim: The n-step actor-critic with a raised policy rate settled near reward 400 while the Monte Carlo baseline agent could not learn faster.
results.setup: CartPole, linear policy (4 weights), Winder's own runs; gamma and learning rates not in the extracted text (equations lost); critic is linear on tile-coded features (605 features)

results.claim: The best state-value decay rate was about 0.1, 0.01 better in the long run, 0.5 unstable, with policy decay rate fixed.
results.setup: n-step actor-critic, CartPole, policy decay rate fixed (value not in text)
results.quote: The results show that the optimal decay rate is approximately 0.1, although a value of 0.01 can eke out greater performance in the long run

results.claim: Tile coding of pole angle and angular velocity (10 cells each, 5 overlaps) gives 605 features for the linear critic.
Shopping cart, single customer, 15 most popular products, 50 epochs: best agent reward 57 of a possible 358.
results.setup: Instacart data, linear eligibility-trace actor-critic, 71 orders, repeated 50 times
results.quote: The highest reward for the agent was 57

results.claim: Across 50 random customers the best agent reward was -1, roughly breaking even.
results.setup: Same agent, 50 random customers, 50 epochs, 15 products
results.quote: This time the agent achieves a maximum reward of –1.

results.claim: A model transferred from random customers took about 200 epochs to match a single-customer agent trained from scratch.
results.quote:
it takes a long time (approximately 200
epochs)

results.claim: Policy gradient algorithms differ only in how the return is estimated.
results.quote:
The only thing that differs between these algorithms is how
you quantify the return.

results.claim: In Pong early episodes score close to -21, so all actions are suppressed without a baseline.
results.setup: Pong, Rainbow DQN example from earlier chapter, illustration
results.quote: Early episodes result in rewards close to –21.

limits: Equations and several hyperparameter values (gamma, learning rates, decay values) were lost in text extraction, so they cannot be checked from the text.
CartPole experiments are simple; author expects little difference between REINFORCE and baseline there.
Shopping cart uses static data with no exploration, a linear model with no memory; author says it is unlikely to perform well in real life.
Transfer result is a single run.
Seeds, hardware and code are not stated.
practices: Try linear approximators before deep learning; they are more robust, faster to train and harder to overfit (n-step example).
The value estimate should learn at least as fast as the policy (n-step example).
Use a library for differentiation rather than by hand (Arbitrary Policies).
Use a sigmoid per action rather than softmax when several actions can be taken at once (Expectations).
Treat the number of pretraining epochs as a hyperparameter when transferring (Results from the Shopping Cart Environment).
Tune decay rates per problem; no single hyperparameters are best (no free lunch).

terms.definition: The policy, which learns and describes the best action to take.
The n-step baseline prediction that criticizes the consequences of the action and is used to update the policy.
Methods to improve the stability of the gradients without affecting learning performance.
